correctness.rationale: Belton defines semiprime density Delta2(t)=a1(t)U(t)+a2(t)/2 with a1=1,a2=0 on 1/2<t<1, so exact branch-normalized density is U(t). For 1/2<t<1, the fractional-part integral gives zeta(t)<0 and derivative bounded by -(1-t)^(-2)+1/t<0; therefore (d/dt)log|zeta(t)|>0. For n>=2, local uniform convergence justifies Möbius/zeta differentiation and interchange with Euler-product log derivative: U_prime=zeta_prime(t)/zeta(t)-sum_{m>=2}Lambda(m)F(m^(-t)), F(z)=sum_{n>=2}mu(n)z^n. For 0<z<=1/sqrt(2), mu(2)=mu(3)=mu(5)=-1 and mu(4)=0, while mu(n)<=1 gives F(z)<=-z^2-z^3-z^5+z^6/(1-z)<0 since z^4/(1-z)<1. Hence U_prime>0 everywhere. At t down to 1/2, n=2 term yields (1/2)log(2t-1)+O(1) -> -infinity; at t up to1, log|zeta(t)|=-log(1-t)+O(1)->+infinity. This proves unique tau with one sign crossing. Integrability of logarithmic endpoint singularities, plus derivative of G(y)=e^(-tau y)B(e^y), gives G_prime=sum-integral of (t-tau)U(t)/t * exp((t-tau)y)>0, and opposite divergent limits; unique integrated zero follows. The supplied verify.py is numerical illustration only; every quantified step above is analytic.
